input.strategy_title: Integrated GenAI model evaluation for RHOAI
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Customers adopting generative models on RHOAI have no supported way to answer
"is this model good enough for my use case?" inside the platform. Evaluation
today happens in ad-hoc notebooks with lm-evaluation-harness or vendor tools,
results live in spreadsheets, and nothing links an evaluation to the model
version that was actually deployed. We need a first-class evaluation capability:
run standard and custom benchmarks against models served on the platform,
persist results alongside the model version, and let users compare candidates
before promoting one to production.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1  | P0 | Users can launch an evaluation of a model served on the platform (KServe endpoint or Llama Stack distribution) against a selected benchmark suite. |
| HLR-2  | P0 | Standard benchmark suites (e.g. MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag exposed through lm-eval task names) are available out of the box. |
| HLR-3  | P0 | Evaluation results are persisted and linked to the Model Registry version of the evaluated model. |
| HLR-4  | P1 | Users can define custom evaluation tasks (own datasets and metrics) and run them through the same flow. |
| HLR-5  | P1 | The Dashboard shows evaluation runs, their status, and per-benchmark scores, and allows side-by-side comparison of two model versions. |
| HLR-6  | P1 | Evaluations can be embedded as a step in a Data Science Pipeline so promotion flows can gate on scores. |
| HLR-7  | P1 | Llama Stack's eval provider API is backed by the platform evaluation service, so agents/apps built on Llama Stack get the same results. |
| HLR-8  | P2 | Evaluation runs record cost/duration metadata (tokens, wall-clock, GPU time) for capacity planning. |
| HLR-9  | P2 | Product documentation covers the evaluation workflow end to end, including custom task authoring. |

## Affected Components

- TrustyAI
- Llama Stack
- Dashboard
- Data Science Pipelines
- Model Registry

## Out of Scope

- Human-preference (arena style) evaluation collection
- Automatic model promotion decisions — pipelines gate, humans promote
- Fine-tuning feedback loops driven by evaluation scores

## Open Questions

1. Execution engine: TrustyAI's LMEvalJob (Tech Preview) already wraps
   lm-evaluation-harness — do we build on it as the single execution path, or is
   a new evaluation service needed to also serve Llama Stack's eval provider
   API? Needs a technical investigation with a recommendation.
2. Result schema: what is the canonical result format persisted to Model
   Registry custom properties, and does it survive benchmark-suite version
   bumps? Prototype against real MMLU output before committing.
3. Benchmark dataset licensing: which standard suites can we redistribute in
   disconnected environments, and which must be fetched by the customer?

# Extend LMEvalJob as the single evaluation execution path

## Description

Conditional plan branch A — applies if the execution engine architecture
investigation recommends building on TrustyAI's LMEvalJob as the single
execution path. This epic extends the LMEvalJob capability so users can launch
an evaluation of a model served on the platform (KServe endpoint or Llama
Stack distribution) against a selected benchmark suite, run custom evaluation
tasks through the same flow, and have results — including cost/duration
metadata — persisted and linked to the Model Registry version of the evaluated
model.

## Scope

- Extend the LMEvalJob-based execution path so an evaluation can be launched
  against a model served on the platform (KServe InferenceService endpoint or
  Llama Stack distribution) with a selected benchmark suite from the standard
  catalog.
- Support custom evaluation tasks (user-defined datasets and metrics) through
  the same launch flow as standard suites.
- Persist evaluation results to Model Registry custom properties on the
  evaluated model's version, in the canonical result schema, including the
  link to the evaluated model version.
- Record cost/duration metadata (tokens, wall-clock, GPU time) in the same
  result record for capacity planning.
- Preserve existing LMEvalJob behavior for current users of the Tech Preview
  capability.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user can launch an evaluation of a model served on the platform against a
  selected benchmark suite, and the evaluation executes via the LMEvalJob
  path.
- Custom evaluation tasks with user-defined datasets and metrics run through
  the same flow as standard suites.
- On completion, results are persisted to Model Registry custom properties on
  the evaluated model version, conforming to the canonical result schema.
- Each evaluation run records tokens, wall-clock time, and GPU time in the
  result record.
- Existing LMEvalJob usage (pre-extension) continues to function.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): users can launch an evaluation of a model served on the
  platform against a selected benchmark suite.
- HLR-3 (P0): evaluation results are persisted and linked to the Model
  Registry version of the evaluated model.
- HLR-4 (P1): users can define custom evaluation tasks and run them through
  the same flow.
- HLR-8 (P2): evaluation runs record cost/duration metadata for capacity
  planning (same result record and persistence surface as HLR-3 — bundled, not
  split).

# New evaluation service for execution and the eval provider API

## Description

Conditional plan branch B — applies if the execution engine architecture
investigation recommends a new evaluation service. This epic builds that
service under the TrustyAI component (the platform's model-quality component):
it exposes the platform's evaluation launch surface, executes evaluations of
models served on the platform (KServe endpoint or Llama Stack distribution)
against selected benchmark suites, supports custom evaluation tasks, persists
results — including cost/duration metadata — linked to the Model Registry
version of the evaluated model, and serves the API surface that Llama Stack's
eval provider backs onto.

## Scope

- Build the evaluation service: an API for launching an evaluation of a model
  served on the platform against a selected benchmark suite, tracking run
  status, and retrieving results.
- Execute evaluations through lm-evaluation-harness-based jobs, reusing the
  existing LMEvalJob runner capabilities where they fit.
- Support custom evaluation tasks (user-defined datasets and metrics) through
  the same launch flow as standard suites.
- Persist evaluation results to Model Registry custom properties on the
  evaluated model's version, in the canonical result schema, including the
  link to the evaluated model version.
- Record cost/duration metadata (tokens, wall-clock, GPU time) in the same
  result record for capacity planning.
- Expose the API surface that the Llama Stack eval provider integration backs
  onto.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user can launch an evaluation of a model served on the platform against a
  selected benchmark suite through the evaluation service API, and the run
  executes and reports status.
- Custom evaluation tasks with user-defined datasets and metrics run through
  the same flow as standard suites.
- On completion, results are persisted to Model Registry custom properties on
  the evaluated model version, conforming to the canonical result schema.
- Each evaluation run records tokens, wall-clock time, and GPU time in the
  result record.
- The service exposes the API surface required to back Llama Stack's eval
  provider.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): users can launch an evaluation of a model served on the
  platform against a selected benchmark suite.
- HLR-3 (P0): evaluation results are persisted and linked to the Model
  Registry version of the evaluated model.
- HLR-4 (P1): users can define custom evaluation tasks and run them through
  the same flow.
- HLR-8 (P2): evaluation runs record cost/duration metadata for capacity
  planning (same result record and persistence surface as HLR-3 — bundled, not
  split).

# Investigation: Evaluation execution engine architecture

## Description

This investigation resolves the strategy's first open question: does the
platform evaluation capability build on TrustyAI's LMEvalJob (Tech Preview,
already wrapping EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness) as the single execution
path, or is a new evaluation service needed that can also serve Llama Stack's
eval provider API? The deliverable is a written recommendation, recorded as an
architecture decision, that determines the shape of every downstream
integration: what surface the Dashboard reads, what the Data Science Pipelines
evaluation step calls, and what the Llama Stack eval provider is backed by.

## Scope

- Analyze the LMEvalJob CRD and the TrustyAI service operator: current
  capabilities, extension points, and limits (multi-suite task selection,
  custom task definitions, result export, API serving).
- Analyze Llama Stack's upstream eval provider API contract and what a
  production eval provider implementation must satisfy.
- Evaluate whether an LMEvalJob-based path can serve all three consumers
  (direct launch by users, pipeline steps, Llama Stack eval provider API) or
  whether a separate evaluation service is required.
- Produce a recommendation with an architecture decision record, including the
  criteria used, the risks of each option, and the explicitly enumerated
  bounded outcomes (extend LMEvalJob vs new evaluation service).
- Identify any follow-on work the chosen option implies for downstream teams
  (Dashboard, Pipelines, Llama Stack).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A recommendation document exists that answers the execution engine question
  with a single selected option and records the decision rationale.
- Each option is evaluated against named criteria: ability to launch
  evaluations against KServe endpoints and Llama Stack distributions, support
  for standard and custom benchmark tasks, ability to serve the Llama Stack
  eval provider API, and result persistence hooks.
- The bounded outcomes are enumerated (extend LMEvalJob as single execution
  path vs new evaluation service) so the conditional downstream plan can be
  resolved.
- Downstream impact on the Dashboard integration, the Data Science Pipelines
  evaluation step, and the Llama Stack eval provider is stated for the
  selected option.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): launching evaluations of served models — gated by this
  investigation's outcome.
- HLR-7 (P1): Llama Stack eval provider API backed by the platform evaluation
  service — gated by this investigation's outcome.

# Investigation: Canonical evaluation result schema

## Description

This investigation resolves the strategy's second open question: what is the
canonical result format persisted to Model Registry custom properties, and
does it survive benchmark-suite version bumps? The deliverable is a validated
schema design, prototyped against real MMLU output before commitment, that
the evaluation execution path will write and the Dashboard, pipeline gating,
and comparison views will consume.

## Scope

- Run lm-evaluation-harness against a real MMLU task and capture the actual
  output structure (per-benchmark scores, aggregation, run metadata).
- Map that output onto Model Registry custom properties on ModelVersion
  entities (the documented extension point), respecting property type and size
  constraints of the Model Registry REST API.
- Design the canonical result record: per-benchmark scores, the link to the
  evaluated model version, and cost/duration metadata (tokens, wall-clock,
  GPU time).
- Analyze schema resilience to benchmark-suite version bumps (field
  additions/renames across lm-eval task versions) and specify a
  versioning/evolution rule.
- Document the schema and the persistence approach as the committed format.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A schema document defines the canonical evaluation result format persisted
  to Model Registry custom properties, including per-benchmark scores and
  cost/duration metadata fields.
- A prototype persisted real MMLU output to Model Registry custom properties
  on a model version using the proposed schema.
- A version-bump analysis demonstrates whether the schema survives
  benchmark-suite version bumps and states the evolution rule; the prototype
  is committed only after this validation passes.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P0): results persisted and linked to the Model Registry version —
  gated by this investigation's outcome.
- HLR-8 (P2): cost/duration metadata in the result record — schema designed
  here.
- HLR-5 (P1): Dashboard per-benchmark score display and comparison — the
  rendered fields are defined by this schema.

# Investigation: Benchmark dataset redistribution licensing

## Description

This investigation resolves the strategy's third open question: which standard
benchmark suites can be redistributed in disconnected environments, and which
must be fetched by the customer? The deliverable is a per-suite licensing
classification that determines the packaging approach of the standard
benchmark suite catalog — bundled with the platform versus documented
customer-side fetch.

## Scope

- Enumerate the candidate standard suites exposed through lm-eval task names
  (e.g. MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag) and the datasets they require.
- Audit each suite's dataset license for redistribution terms in
  disconnected/air-gapped delivery.
- Classify each suite: redistributable (can ship in the platform catalog) vs
  customer-fetched (documented fetch path required).
- Record the classification with license citations and the resulting packaging
  guidance for the standard suite catalog.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every candidate standard suite has a documented classification
  (redistributable vs customer-fetched) with a citation of the governing
  license.
- The classification covers disconnected-environment delivery explicitly.
- Packaging guidance for the standard suite catalog is stated so the catalog
  implementation can proceed without further licensing decisions.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): standard benchmark suites available out of the box — the
  delivery mechanism (bundled vs customer-fetched) is gated by this
  investigation's outcome.

# Standard benchmark suite catalog and packaging

## Description

This epic delivers the out-of-the-box standard benchmark suites for the
platform evaluation capability. Standard suites exposed through lm-eval task
names (e.g. MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag) become selectable evaluation targets, with
each suite packaged according to its redistribution licensing classification:
bundled with the platform where redistribution is permitted, or delivered via
a documented customer-side fetch mechanism where it is not.

## Scope

- Build the standard suite catalog: the set of lm-eval task configurations
  selectable when launching an evaluation of a served model.
- Package redistributable suites so they work in disconnected environments
  without customer-side dataset setup.
- Provide the documented fetch path for suites whose datasets cannot be
  redistributed, with clear failure messaging when a suite is not yet fetched.
- Align catalog contents with the per-suite licensing classification produced
  by the benchmark dataset licensing investigation.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user launching an evaluation of a model served on the platform can select
  each named standard suite (MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag) from the catalog.
- Suites classified redistributable run against a served model in a
  disconnected environment with no customer-side dataset setup.
- Suites classified customer-fetched have a documented fetch mechanism, and
  attempting to run one before fetching produces an actionable error.
- No suite is bundled in violation of its dataset license.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): standard benchmark suites available out of the box.

# Evaluation step for Data Science Pipelines

## Description

This epic makes evaluation embeddable as a step in a Data Science Pipeline, so
promotion flows can gate on benchmark scores: a pipeline run launches an
evaluation of a served model against a benchmark suite and exposes the
resulting scores as step outputs that downstream gating logic can consume.
Humans still make promotion decisions; the pipeline only gates.

## Scope

- Provide a Kubeflow Pipelines (v2) component that launches an evaluation of a
  specified served model against a specified benchmark suite through the
  platform's chosen execution path (per the execution engine architecture
  decision).
- Expose evaluation status and per-benchmark scores as component outputs so
  subsequent pipeline steps can gate on them (fail or branch on thresholds).
- Ensure the component works within DataSciencePipelinesApplication-managed
  project pipelines.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A Data Science Pipeline run can include an evaluation step that launches an
  evaluation of a served model and waits for its completion.
- Per-benchmark scores are available as step outputs to downstream pipeline
  steps.
- A pipeline can be authored so a subsequent step fails or branches when a
  score is below a configured threshold.
- The evaluation step runs within a project's Data Science Pipelines
  application without manual cluster-level setup.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-6 (P1): evaluations can be embedded as a step in a Data Science
  Pipeline so promotion flows can gate on scores.

**Overall:** This is a strong decomposition that navigates the strategy's central trap cleanly and produces a coherent, well-gated multi-team DAG. It has several minor blemishes — most self-identified — but no material gap.

**1. HLR coverage — solid.** All nine HLRs map to epics: HLR-1/3/4/8 to the conditional branch epics (both branches carry all four, so coverage holds regardless of the E001 outcome), HLR-2 to E004, HLR-5/6/7 to E005/E006/E007, HLR-9 to E008. The HLR-1+4 and HLR-3+8 bundling is justified by the strategy's own "through the same flow" wording and the shared result record — not a deferral or priority collapse. Out-of-scope items are respected (E006 explicitly keeps humans in promotion decisions; no arena or fine-tuning feedback work appears).

**2. Epic boundaries — one flagged weakness.** Component/team tuples are clean, Model Registry is correctly treated as passive (investigation only), no sibling duplicates a data structure or surface, and E008 is pure content authoring. The weakness is BRANCH-B-E009: a greenfield service bundling API, execution, custom tasks, persistence, and the provider-API surface in one epic — the decomposition's own Health Warning 6 admits it may exceed a sprint, and the ~2-week target is likely not met. Mitigating factors keep this minor rather than material: it is a conditional plan document (not committed scope), one team and one codebase, heavily reusing existing building blocks, with an explicit split-at-estimation plan. Still, it's the clearest rubric deviation in the set.

**3. DAG quality — solid with one rationale gap.** Every Mermaid edge matches frontmatter dependencies in both directions, arrows run dependency → dependent, no cycles, no main-plan epic depends on a branch node, and both branches correctly set `branch` and `gated_by` with populated `gate_failure_impact` (true rewrite gates, not scheduling dependencies). Docs-last edges (E004/E005/E006/E007 → E008) are present; E001 → E008 as the branch proxy is justified. Parallelism is right: three independent investigations fan out to parallel implementations, critical path 3 is reasonable. The gap: the justification for no E004 ↔ branch-epic edges cites Rule 14 (different repos), which doesn't cover the same-repo TrustyAI pair consuming the catalog at runtime. The parallelization itself is defensible (the catalog is runtime data, generic over lm-eval task names, outcome-independent), but the cited rule doesn't actually support the claim as written.

**4. Scope fidelity — excellent; the annotated trap is avoided.** The strategy deliberately does not choose the execution engine or the result schema, and no epic hardcodes either: E001 investigates the engine with both bounded outcomes represented as conditional branches mirroring the strategy's own open-question framing; E002 investigates the schema; E005/E006/E007/E008 all reference "the chosen execution path" and "the canonical result schema" abstractly. No epic body references sibling draft IDs; cross-references use descriptive phrases.

**5. Acceptance criteria — solid.** Every epic's ACs are concrete and testable, traceable to HLRs, and rule-mandated ACs are present where applicable: E005's feature flag, E008's technical review by owning engineers, Branch A's backwards-compatibility AC for the Tech Preview foundation, and E002's prototype-against-real-MMLU-output AC carrying the strategy's explicit wording. No soft ACs. One small misalignment: E008's docs scope promises cost/duration metadata display "in the Dashboard," but E005 implements no such rendering and no HLR requires the display — E008's scope overreaches E005's deliverable slightly.

One epic in the set is scored against a different convention; either reading is coherent, the mixture is not.

**Scoring:** No P0 is uncovered, the DAG is coherent, scope fidelity is clean, and ACs are strong. But "all five dimensions solid" (a 5) is precluded by the BRANCH-B-E009 breadth concern, the incomplete DAG justification for the E004/branch parallelism, the signal-convention inconsistency, and the E008/E005 cost-display misalignment. None of these individually rises to a material gap — the branch epic is a flagged, mitigated conditional-plan breadth issue rather than a committed multi-sprint monolith, and the DAG edge absence is correct even if its cited rule is incomplete.
